formattedActions.title: Establish Multilevel Commitments and Platforms for Climate Investment
formattedActions.description: This action helps national governments align national climate commitments with city and subnational priorities and establish platforms for coordinated implementation and investment. It supports governments to translate NDCs and other national commitments into shared priorities, clarify responsibilities, and connect local investment needs with national and international support.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Climate investment requires shared priorities and sustained coordination across government levels. Joint commitments can connect NDCs and other national goals with local priorities, responsibilities, and investment needs. National coordination mechanisms can facilitate ongoing collaboration between governments and wider implementation actors. Country platforms can then connect urban priorities with national investment strategies and finance partners. Together, these mechanisms create the institutional foundations for investment planning, finance mobilization, and implementation.

pathways.title: 1.1 Multilevel Climate Commitments
pathways.overview: Multilevel climate commitments align national, subnational, and city governments around shared climate priorities, responsibilities and financing needs. These commitments can be embedded in existing NDCs, NAPs, and national climate strategies, or established through complementary agreements and processes. They help connect national climate goals with local priorities, investment needs, and implementation responsibilities, creating a clearer basis for coordinating climate finance and action across government levels.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Embed multilevel commitments within NDCs, NAPs or national climate strategies, or establish new agreements where existing processes are insufficient.

Consider setting a small set of core commitments for participating governments, while allowing them to make additional or more ambitious commitments based on their priorities, capacities, and readiness.
Consider whether to engage cities directly, through subnational government associations or through phased participation, depending on your country's governance arrangements and local capacities.

Consider whether a dedicated urban climate investment and implementation strategy is needed, or whether existing national, sectoral, and subnational plans can provide a sufficient framework for implementation.

implementationGuidance.title: Assess existing national commitments
implementationGuidance.content: Review NDCs, NAPs, national urban policies, and relevant sectoral strategies to identify existing existing climate targets, investment priorities and financing commitments involving cities and subnational governments, as well as gaps in their inclusion.

implementationGuidance.title: Facilitate subnational commitments
implementationGuidance.content: Support cities and subnational governments in developing climate commitments and investment strategies where these are absent, building on their existing climate priorities and plans, assessed investment needs, and institutional capacities.

implementationGuidance.title: Define complementary commitments and responsibilities
implementationGuidance.content: Work with subnational governments to establish complementary climate and investment targets, milestones and financing responsibilities. Clarify institutional responsibilities for mobilizing resources and leading delivery across government levels.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect commitments to investment planning
implementationGuidance.content: Translate shared commitments into actionable investment priorities, portfolios, and pipelines, and integrate these into national and subnational budgeting (see Pathways 3.1 and 3.2).

relatedPathways.title: 3.1 Local Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning

implementationGuidance.title: Review and update commitments
implementationGuidance.content: Regularly assess progress, financing needs, and implementation barriers. Use findings to update commitments and inform subsequent national and subnational planning, including future NDC revision and implementation cycles.

illustrativeExamples.title: Chile – 2025 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Chile’s 2025 NDC includes specific subnational commitments covering regional and municipal climate plans, institutional capacity, and climate finance. Notably, the country commits to establishing a national network to identify, mobilize, and deploy subnational climate finance, with active participation from subnational governments. The NDC assigns responsibilities and deadlines for these commitments across government levels, creating a framework to link national ambition with local planning, finance, and implementation.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Chile shows how multilevel climate and investment commitments can be embedded within an NDC.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Climate City Contract 2030
illustrativeExamples.fullText: As part of the Climate City Contracts, Swedish municipalities, national government agencies, and Viable Cities make commitments around a shared climate-neutrality mission and review them annually. The contracts connect climate goals with portfolios of projects and investment planning. The process has expanded from nine municipalities in 2019 to 48 municipalities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Sweden shows how an iterative multilevel commitment process can link shared climate and investment goals across national and subnational governments.

illustrativeExamples.title: Rwanda – Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Rwanda's nationally determined contribution (NDC) 3.0 commits to developing climate investment plans that can be implemented across all of the country’s 30 districts. The Rwanda Green Fund (RGF) and district authorities are among the institutions responsible for financing and implementing this commitment. The RGF already mobilizes climate finance and manages facilities that can finance national and local public-sector climate investments. This creates an institutional bridge between national climate commitments, district investment planning, and Rwanda's wider climate-finance architecture.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Rwanda shows how an NDC can connect national climate commitments with subnational investment planning and a national institution to mobilize and deploy climate finance.

illustrativeExamples.title: Global – Sustainable Urban Resilience for the Next Generation (SURGe) Initiative
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Launched at COP27 under the Egyptian Presidency, in collaboration with UN-Habitat and facilitated by ICLEI, SURGe brings together national and local governments, city networks and other partners to accelerate urban climate action. Through its Global Alliance and five sectoral tracks covering buildings and housing, urban energy, waste, mobility and water, the initiative aims to strengthen the recognition of local climate commitments in NDCs and support coordinated implementation. Its objectives also include working with national governments to develop context-specific financing mechanisms, connecting cities with development banks and climate funds, and supporting urban project pipelines. SURGe therefore illustrates how international partnerships can connect national climate ambition with local commitments, sectoral priorities and financing opportunities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: SURGe shows how international initiatives can support multilevel climate commitments, sectoral collaboration and access to finance for urban climate action.

illustrativeExamples.title: UN-Habitat – Seizing the Urban Opportunity: A 3-Step Guide for Strengthening NDCs 3.0
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Co-developed by UN-Habitat and SDU Resilience, this guide provides a three-step methodology to assess, prepare and co-design NDCs with stronger urban climate commitments. It helps governments review existing NDCs and national and subnational policies, identify financing opportunities, and strengthen multilevel governance arrangements. It also supports engagement with sector ministries and local stakeholders to align priorities and clarify institutional responsibilities. The co-design process helps governments identify urban mitigation and adaptation actions across sectors and incorporate the finance, technology and capacity-building support needed for implementation into national commitments. The guide can also inform NDC implementation planning and future revisions by helping governments identify relevant urban commitments, responsible actors and remaining gaps.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Strengthen national climate commitments by integrating urban priorities, subnational contributions and implementation needs into NDCs through multilevel and cross-sectoral collaboration.

illustrativeExamples.title: UN-Habitat – Urban Content in NDC 3.0: Cities at the Centre
illustrativeExamples.fullText: UN-Habitat's analysis examines the urban content of third-generation NDCs. It assesses how national climate plans address cities across mitigation and adaptation sectors, multilevel governance, financing, and implementation. It also examines changes across NDC revision cycles, providing an evidence base for governments seeking to strengthen urban climate commitments.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Understand how urban priorities, sectoral commitments, and implementation arrangements are reflected in NDCs and identify opportunities for improvement.

illustrativeExamples.title: ICAT – Climate Action Aggregation Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by the Initiative for Climate Action Transparency, the Climate Action Aggregation Tool (CAAT) outlines a step-by-step process for national governments to quantify the aggregate GHG impact of climate actions by cities, regions, and other non-state actors. It also accounts for overlaps between actions and national policies. National governments can use CAAT to incorporate subnational action into national climate targets, NDC development, and investment planning.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: This tool shows how subnational climate commitments could contribute to national targets and incorporate them into NDC and investment planning.

pathways.title: 1.2 National Coordination Mechanisms
pathways.overview: National coordination mechanisms provide a structure for national and subnational governments to coordinate climate investment and implementation. They connect local priorities with national policies, programs, finance, and technical support. They can also enable whole-of-society engagement, bringing in businesses, financial institutions, academia, civil society and communities where needed. To sustain this coordination, mechanisms can include dedicated capacity to convene actors day-to-day, follow up on financing and implementation needs, and bring local feedback into national decision-making.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Establish the coordination mechanism suited to the governance system and institutional capacities – this could be a national coordination platform, recurring dialogue series, or other arrangements.

Depending on institutional mandates and coordination capacities, you can lead coordination nationally, share leadership across government levels or engage intermediaries such as city networks to facilitate the process.

Where cities have different levels of technical and institutional capacity, consider providing additional support to ensure that lower-capacity municipalities can participate effectively in coordination and investment discussions.

Involve different national institutions and external partners depending on the issues being addressed. Financing challenges may require finance ministries, development banks, and investors, while sector-specific barriers may also require sector ministries.

implementationGuidance.title: Build on existing processes
implementationGuidance.content: Identify where climate planning, budgeting, and financing decisions already take place. Strengthen related existing processes rather than creating additional coordination mechanisms.

implementationGuidance.title: Clarify institutional roles
implementationGuidance.content: Define which national ministries and subnational institutions are responsible for financing, regulating, and implementing priority climate actions. Identify shared responsibilities and coordination needs across government levels and sectors.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage actors beyond government
implementationGuidance.content: Identify businesses, financial institutions, academia, civil society, and community actors that influence climate action. Bring them into the coordination process to contribute finance, expertise, assets, and implementation capacity.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect coordination to investment decisions
implementationGuidance.content: Use coordination mechanisms to identify investment needs, and mobilize investors, technical assistance providers, and decision-makers for implementation (see Pathways 1.3, 3.1 and 3.2).

relatedPathways.title: 3.1 Local Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning

implementationGuidance.title: Sustain coordination
implementationGuidance.content: Identify a team or institution to convene actors, track local needs, and agreed actions, and facilitate follow-up across national and subnational governments.

implementationGuidance.title: Review progress and improve
implementationGuidance.content: Regularly review implementation and financing barriers with subnational governments. Where needed, adjust shared commitments based on the reviews and feed lessons into policy or institutional reforms, program designs, funding decisions, and subsequent coordination cycles (see Pathway 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2).

relatedPathways.title: 2.2 Reform Roadmaps for Urban Climate Investment

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Viability Fund for Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Viability Fund for Cities is an emerging mechanism to coordinate funding from different public and private funders toward urban climate investment portfolios. Building on Sweden's Viable Cities experience, it is being developed around three interconnected functions: ALIGN, bringing funders and implementation partners around shared climate transition portfolios and place-based interventions; CO-FINANCE, mobilizing catalytic capital and coordinating contributions from different financing partners toward local investments; and DEMAND, aggregating purchasing demand to shape markets and support deployment of climate solutions. The initiative aims to mobilize EUR 10 billion in co-financing and EUR 10 billion in aggregated demand by 2030, through partnerships across national, subnational, and international levels. Its institutional and financing arrangements remain under development and are intended to be adapted to different country contexts.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Sweden shows how a multilevel coordination mechanism is being developed to align different funding sources for urban climate investment portfolios and connect financing with market demand.

illustrativeExamples.title: Croatia – National Multilevel Climate and Energy Dialogue
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Between 2022 and 2025, Croatia’s North-West Croatia Regional Energy and Climate Agency (REGEA) facilitated six multilevel climate and energy dialogues involving cities and regions, nine national ministries, businesses, academia, and civil society. Initially focused on Croatia's National Energy and Climate Plan, the dialogues evolved to address practical barriers to local implementation, including access to finance. A dedicated dialogue on financing brought municipalities together with the Ministry of Finance and financial-sector actors to discuss how local climate plans could be funded. These discussions led to the creation of the Platform for Sustainable Finance and Energy Transition, providing a space to connect local financing needs with national and financial-sector actors. Croatia is working to institutionalize the multilevel dialogue through an inter-ministerial structure involving national and municipal representatives.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Croatia shows how multilevel coordination can help national governments to identify subnational financing barriers and translate them into new institutional responses.

illustrativeExamples.title: Brazil, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan – CCFLA Local Hubs
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CCFLA Local Hub for Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan convened 25 local governments, 10 national agencies, and project preparation partners, including the Gap Fund and FELICITY II, to identify building-decarbonization projects and connect cities with technical support. In Brazil, the Local Hub brings together over 50 local, national and international partners, supporting coordination through a community of practice and the Green and Resilient Cities Programme (PCVR) Project Bank. These arrangements help strengthen connections between municipal investment needs, national institutions, and potential financing partners.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: CCFLA Local Hubs show how intermediary platforms can support multilevel coordination and connect municipal climate investment priorities with project preparation and financing partners.

pathways.title: 1.3 Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms
pathways.overview: Urban-inclusive country platforms bring city and subnational priorities into nationally led processes for mobilizing climate and development finance. Country platforms align governments and development partners around shared missions, such as climate action. Cities and subnational governments, however, are often not systematically represented in these platforms, despite their important roles in climate action. Urban-inclusive platforms can address this gap by integrating urban and subnational priorities into platform governance, investment planning, and financing. This can align national and local climate plans, strengthen urban project pipelines, and mobilize public, development, and private finance for local climate action. Participation in country platforms can also bring cities and subnational governments closer to global climate finance platforms and international partners, creating opportunities to access technical assistance, partnerships and financing support.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Assign leadership to finance or planning ministries or other national government institutions, depending on national responsibilities for investment planning and finance mobilization.
Consider whether cities should participate directly or through regional governments, or city coalitions, depending on your country's governance system and number of jurisdictions.
Consider whether small cities and those with limited technical or financial capacities may need additional project preparation support or financial intermediation to participate effectively.
Begin with investment portfolios in priority sectors and expand over time. Financing arrangements should reflect local borrowing powers, creditworthiness, and access to capital.

implementationGuidance.title: Establish national ownership and mandate
implementationGuidance.content: Identify the national institution or group responsible for leading the platform. Define its purpose, responsibilities, and relationship with existing government processes.

implementationGuidance.title: Create entry points for cities
implementationGuidance.content: Establish institutional arrangements for cities and subnational governments to bring finance and implementation needs into national discussions.

implementationGuidance.title: Align investment priorities
implementationGuidance.content: Connect national climate and development objectives with city plans, investment portfolios, and project pipelines (see Pathways 1.1, 3.1, 3.2).

relatedPathways.title: 3.1 Local Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning

implementationGuidance.title: Coordinate project preparation support
implementationGuidance.content: Engage project preparation facilities and development partners to strengthen urban pipelines and explore aggregation of smaller projects (see Pathway 3.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Engage financing partners
implementationGuidance.content: Bring national and multilateral development banks, climate funds, and private financiers around urban investment needs. Identify suitable public, concessional, and private financing instruments (see Pathway 4.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Monitor progress and adapt support
implementationGuidance.content: Track the implementation of urban or subnational portfolios. Use findings to adjust national support arrangements.

illustrativeExamples.title: Cameroon – Finance Your Cities Country Platform for Localizing Finance
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Announced at COP30, Cameroon’s country platform brings national ministries, local and regional governments and the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM), Cameroon’s municipal financing institution, around a shared pipeline of climate and development projects. The platform aims to align national policies and investment plans with local climate priorities. FEICOM acts as a financial intermediary between cities and finance providers, aiming to connect local projects with private and international capital, as part of a portfolio approach.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Cameroon shows how a country platform can integrate urban investment priorities into the national financial architecture, supported by a domestic financial intermediary.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – Just Energy Transition Partnership (JET-P)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: South Africa’s Just Energy Transition Partnership mobilizes international support around the country’s transition, guided by its Just Energy Transition Investment and Implementation Plans. Municipalities have a dedicated portfolio within the platform, reflecting their major role in electricity distribution, energy access and local infrastructure. A JET Municipal Council, led by the South African Local Government Association, provides a route for municipal participation in the country platform. It brings together municipal representatives, national ministries, the National Treasury, the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) and other energy-sector institutions. Through three workstreams covering municipal capability, financing and energy access, the council identifies investment priorities, develops project pipelines and explores financing options for municipal infrastructure. Dedicated programs within the municipal portfolio also support municipalities with project preparation and access to concessional and private finance.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: South Africa shows how a country platform can integrate municipalities into national investment coordination and support portfolios, project preparation and financing.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Viable Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Launched in 2017, Viable Cities serves as Sweden's mission-oriented country platform, connecting 48 municipalities, six national government agencies and wider societal actors around the mission of climate-neutral cities by 2030. The agencies are the Swedish Energy Agency, Vinnova, Formas, the Swedish Agency for Economic and Regional Growth, the Swedish Transport Administration and the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency.
At its core, Climate City Contract 2030 (CCC) provides an annual process for renewing complementary national–local commitments and connecting municipal climate priorities and investment needs with opportunities for national support. Municipalities work to integrate climate priorities into planning, budgeting and procurement, while Transition Arenas engage businesses, academia and civil society in local transitions.
Viable Cities supports these processes through research and innovation funding, tools, methods and peer learning, while cities contribute staff and municipal resources. Its Coordination Function identifies municipal and regional needs, facilitates multilevel collaboration and helps align national and European initiatives. Building on this established capacity, Viable Cities is developing stronger links to investment preparation, financing and market demand, including through the emerging Viability Fund for Cities and Local Investment Structures, which remain under development and do not imply finance already mobilized at scale. These will aim to complement existing financing mechanisms, such as Kommuninvest's direct lending to eligible municipal borrowers. Notably, Viable Cities facilitates coordination, while investment and financing decisions remain with the responsible actors and appropriately mandated financial institutions. 
Viable Cities' experience has also informed knowledge exchange and related national platform development under the EU Cities Mission.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Sweden shows how a mission-oriented country platform can enable multilevel coordination around climate action planning, investment, and implementation.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA and Global SDSN Commission – Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms Framework
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CCFLA’s framework provides guidance on how a country platform can be designed to systematically integrate cities and subnational priorities into country-platform governance, investment planning, and financing. It addresses common barriers, including misalignment between national and local priorities, weak urban project pipelines, limited fiscal capacity and creditworthiness, and a lack of city-focused financial instruments. The framework’s phased roadmap covers whole-of-government engagement, program readiness, investment programming, financing, and implementation. It identifies practical approaches for engaging cities and subnational governments, strengthening urban investment pipelines, aggregating smaller projects, and connecting them with appropriate financing instruments through national and local financial institutions.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: This framework identifies a practical roadmap for integrating urban and subnational priorities, investment pipelines, and financing needs into country platforms.

illustrativeExamples.title: Viability Fund for Cities – Country Platform Functions
illustrativeExamples.fullText: This guide supports the [CHAMP Implementation Roadmap 2026–2028](https://www.champ-climate.org/champ-implementation-roadmap-2026-2028) through country platforms that coordinate locally owned portfolios. Drawing on Viable Cities and Climate City Contract 2030, it connects recurring commitments, coordination and learning with demonstrators, local investment structures and demand programmes. Platforms can coordinate preparation and national investment portfolios, connect domestic and international finance, and address institutional barriers. Receiving and channelling funding requires appropriate mandates and financial arrangements. The approach links implementation evidence with policy, support and country-led review.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Connect locally owned climate portfolios with national priorities, preparation support, finance and delivery.

formattedActions.title: Strengthen Enabling Environments for Climate Investment
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to identify and address barriers to urban climate finance and implementation. These may include policy, financing, data and coordination barriers. Governments can use these findings to prioritize reforms that improve investment conditions for cities.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Mobilizing urban climate finance requires more than the availability of capital. Policies, institutions, fiscal frameworks, and regulatory conditions influence whether cities can prepare, finance, and implement climate projects. National governments can address systemic barriers that cities cannot resolve alone, including borrowing restrictions, regulatory constraints, and gaps in financial frameworks. Assessing these barriers and implementing targeted reforms can improve cities’ investment readiness, access to finance, and capacity to implement climate projects.

pathways.title: 2.1 Enabling Framework Conditions Assessments
pathways.overview: Enabling framework conditions assessments help national and subnational governments to systematically identify barriers to urban climate investment. Through evidence collection and stakeholder engagement, they reveal how existing conditions across data, finance, and governance affect investment and implementation across government levels. Findings can help governments identify reform priorities requiring coordinated national and subnational action.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Match the scope and depth of the assessment to available institutional capacity. Where capacities are limited, begin with priority sectors or investment barriers and expand over time.
Adapt the assessment to available data. Where climate, fiscal, or investment data are limited, use stakeholder consultations and qualitative evidence.
Involve national and subnational institutions with the mandate, political support, and capacity to act on the findings so that assessments can inform reforms in investment conditions.

implementationGuidance.title: Define the scope of the assessment
implementationGuidance.content: Identify the investment challenges the assessment should examine. Determine which institutions, government levels, and financing systems should be included.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage subnational governments early
implementationGuidance.content: While developing the purpose and scope of the assessment, involve cities and subnational authorities early to identify their specific investment challenges and priorities.

implementationGuidance.title: Assess existing conditions
implementationGuidance.content: Review relevant policies, fiscal systems, financing frameworks, institutional arrangements, and data, including alignment between NDCs, national urban policies, and relevant sectoral strategies. Validate findings through stakeholder consultations.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify investment barriers
implementationGuidance.content: Determine which policy, fiscal, institutional, financing, or data constraints are limiting urban climate investment. Distinguish national barriers from those that can be addressed locally.

implementationGuidance.title: Validate findings across government levels
implementationGuidance.content: Discuss findings with cities, subnational governments, and relevant national institutions. Use this process to confirm reform priorities, identify areas requiring joint action, and inform updates to shared climate commitments where relevant (see Pathway 1.1).

implementationGuidance.title: Prioritize areas for reform
implementationGuidance.content: Identify which barriers have the greatest effect on investment and implementation. Use the findings to inform reform priorities, technical assistance, and financing support (see Pathway 2.2).

relatedPathways.title: 2.2 Reform Roadmaps for Urban Climate Investment

implementationGuidance.title: Repeat the assessment when needed
implementationGuidance.content: Revisit priority areas as reforms progress and investment conditions change.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – National Enabling Framework Conditions Assessment
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The National Enabling Framework Conditions assessment was piloted by GIZ in collaboration with India's Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the National Institute of Urban Affairs, and the Energy and Resources Institute. It included a desk review with seven stakeholder interviews and two roundtables in New Delhi attended by more than 80 participants. The assessment identified gaps across four dimensions, including local institutional mandates, own-source revenues and borrowings, city-level climate data, and coordination between state and local governments. Each gap points to a specific reform — broadening grants from the national finance commission to support climate action, for instance, or issuing city climate action plan guidelines under national missions.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: India shows how a national assessment can identify policy, fiscal, data, and institutional barriers to urban climate finance and inform reform priorities.

illustrativeExamples.title: Indonesia – Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions Assessment
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Conducted under the Urban-Act project, the subnational National Enabling Framework Conditions assessment covered Medan City, Binjai City, and Deli Serdang Regency (Mebidang) in North Sumatra, Indonesia. It identified progress in integrating climate priorities into local development plans and using intergovernmental transfers for climate action. However, gaps remain in municipal climate budgeting, access to private and innovative finance, climate data, and coordination across government levels. The assessment recommended extending climate budget tagging to municipalities, strengthening local revenue and financing options, and establishing a coordination team led by North Sumatra's Development Planning Agency. These recommendations aim to strengthen local financing conditions and align climate planning and implementation across government levels.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Indonesia shows how a subnational assessment can identify progress and gaps in policy, financing, and coordination and recommend improvements through multilevel action.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions Assessment
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Conducted in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, the subnational National Enabling Framework Conditions assessment examined climate policy, budgeting and finance, climate data, and multilevel coordination. It identified existing strengths, including Tamil Nadu's climate policies and financing institutions, and Coimbatore's Climate Resilient City Action Plan. However, gaps remain in city-level climate budgeting, access to finance, climate data, and alignment between state and municipal planning. The assessment recommended strengthening climate budgeting, expanding state support for municipal climate investment, and improving coordination between state and city institutions.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: India shows how a city-level assessment can identify barriers and opportunities for strengthening climate finance and coordination between state and municipal institutions.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA – National Enabling Framework Conditions Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The tool assesses national enabling conditions for urban climate finance across four categories: policy, budget and finance, climate data, and vertical and horizontal coordination. Through evidence collection, stakeholder consultations, and analysis, the tool helps national governments understand existing enabling conditions, identify barriers to urban climate investment, and prioritize areas for reform.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Assess national policy, fiscal, and institutional barriers to urban climate finance and identify reform priorities requiring national action.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA – Subnational Enabling Framework Conditions Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The tool is designed primarily for subnational and municipal governments. It assesses enabling conditions for urban climate finance at the city, metropolitan, state, or regional level. Through evidence collection, stakeholder consultations, and analysis, it helps subnational governments identify strengths, investment barriers and areas for improvement. Used alongside the National EFC Tool, it helps identify barriers requiring action at different government levels.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Assess local conditions affecting access to climate finance and identify improvements requiring subnational action.

pathways.title: 2.2 Reform Roadmaps for Urban Climate Investment
pathways.overview: Enabling reforms help governments to address policy, regulatory and institutional barriers that constrain urban climate finance and implementation. Building on enabling framework conditions assessments (Pathway 2.1), national and subnational governments can develop reform roadmaps that identify priority actions, institutional responsibilities, resources and implementation milestones. These roadmaps can help to sequence reforms across government institutions and coordinate financial and technical support for implementation.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Account for any parliamentary approvals, legislative changes, and intergovernmental agreements that may be needed to implement reforms.

Adapt reform responsibilities to the country's governance structure. Centralized structures may require stronger national leadership, while decentralized structures may require greater subnational ownership and coordination.

Consider fiscal space and municipal capacities. The availability of national grants, development finance and performance-linked incentives could catalyze municipal reforms. Municipalities with limited capacities may require phased reforms, technical assistance, and additional implementation support.

implementationGuidance.title: Prioritize feasible reforms
implementationGuidance.content: Identify barriers with the greatest effect on urban climate investment, then prioritize reforms to address them based on urgency, political feasibility, and potential benefits (see Pathway 2.1).

implementationGuidance.title: Define priority actions
implementationGuidance.content: Specify the actions required for each reform and identify the responsible national and subnational institutions. Define milestones, resources, and technical support where needed.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify dependencies
implementationGuidance.content: Determine which reforms require national action and which can be implemented locally. Sequence connected reforms and use national coordination mechanisms to address institutional dependencies (see Pathway 1.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Connect reforms with finance
implementationGuidance.content: Identify where public funding, development finance, technical assistance, or performance-based incentives can support implementation.

implementationGuidance.title: Track progress and revise
implementationGuidance.content: Establish clear milestones and review progress periodically. Update priorities when reforms advance, or new barriers emerge.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – Metro Trading Services Reform Program
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Metro Trading Services Reform Program, led by South Africa’s National Treasury in collaboration with relevant national departments, targets the country’s eight metropolitan municipalities. It provides performance-based conditional grants to incentivize improvements in water supply and sanitation, electricity and energy, and solid waste management. Participating municipalities develop Trading Services Reform Strategies, which include institutional roadmaps and business and investment plans that identify institutional changes, financing needs, and service delivery priorities. These strategies must be approved by the municipal council and also include city-level Performance Improvement Action Plans with measurable reform targets, against which progress is independently verified. A six-year ZAR 54 billion performance-linked grant provides incentives to participating municipalities, with funding tied to progress against agreed targets. By strengthening municipal governance, revenue management, and financial sustainability, the program aims to increase investment in essential urban infrastructure, including climate-relevant services.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: South Africa shows how national governments can connect municipal reform roadmaps with performance-linked financing to improve infrastructure investment conditions.

illustrativeExamples.title: Uganda – Support to Municipal Infrastructure Development (USMID)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Led by the Ministry of Lands, Housing, and Urban Development, USMID began in 2013 with 14 municipalities and later expanded to additional local governments. As part of USMID, technical, financial, and institutional assessments in local governments informed a Programme Action Plan, outlining corrective actions, institutional responsibilities, and implementation timelines. Municipalities also developed capacity-building plans addressing weaknesses in planning, revenue management, procurement, and infrastructure delivery. Annual performance assessments linked municipal infrastructure grants to improvements in institutional performance and implementation. USMID closed in 2024 with a satisfactory outcome rating. Building on this experience, Uganda secured USD 540 million in World Bank financing in 2026 for the successor Uganda Cities and Municipalities Infrastructure Development program, expanding support for municipal institutions and climate-smart infrastructure.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Uganda shows how national governments can use institutional assessments, municipal improvement plans, and performance-linked financing to strengthen urban investment conditions.

illustrativeExamples.title: Climate Policy Initiative – The Brazil Climate Finance Reform Compass
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Brazil Climate Finance Reform Compass: The Compass adapts the global framework to the national context, identifying gaps and reform priorities across the same nine thematic areas and mapping the institutions, actors, and milestones needed to advance them. Both are designed as living tools that can be updated as policies, evidence, and stakeholder priorities evolve, helping governments and other stakeholders coordinate reforms, track progress, and strengthen alignment between climate finance and broader development priorities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: See how a climate-finance reform framework can be tailored to national institutions, priorities, and decision-making processes.

formattedActions.title: Plan, Prepare and Implement Climate Investment Portfolios
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to work with cities and subnational governments to translate shared climate priorities into coordinated project portfolios, finance-ready project pipelines and implementation. It covers climate budgeting and investment planning, portfolio and pipeline development, project preparation, and place-based environments for implementing project portfolios.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Climate priorities need to become clear investment opportunities before finance can be mobilized. To this end, investment planning and budgeting identify investment needs, responsibilities and available resources. Portfolio development combines projects with the policy, governance and other interventions needed for delivery, while identifying investment opportunities that can form project pipelines. Project preparation helps suitable investments to become finance-ready, while collaborative implementation environments bring actors together to address systemic barriers, test solutions and advance interconnected interventions. These processes reinforce one another as portfolios evolve.

pathways.title: 3.1 Local Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning
pathways.overview: Local climate budgeting and investment planning help cities to integrate climate priorities into public spending and investment decisions. Climate action plans do not always identify investment costs, financing responsibilities, or links to government budgets, making implementation difficult. Climate budgeting helps to integrate local climate targets into municipal and subnational budget planning, allocations, implementation, and expenditure monitoring. It can be informed by multiyear capital investment planning, which identifies future investment needs, costs, and available resources. National governments can enable these processes by working with subnational governments to develop common budget taxonomies, supportive public-finance regulations, and reporting standards, alongside technical assistance.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Adapt climate budgeting approaches to local fiscal autonomy and national public-finance requirements.
Promote municipal budget tagging and basic investment-cost estimates where municipal capacities are limited, using findings to inform national technical assistance and capacity building.

implementationGuidance.title: Establish enabling frameworks for local climate budgeting
implementationGuidance.content: Work with subnational governments to develop common climate budget taxonomies, methodologies, and reporting standards. Where needed, align national accounting rules, budget formats, and fiscal regulations to enable their integration into municipal budgeting and capital investment planning (see Pathway 1.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Support climate-informed investment planning
implementationGuidance.content: Provide guidance and technical assistance to help cities estimate climate investment costs, assess available resources and funding gaps, and prioritize investments in multiyear financial and capital investment plans. Identify where national funding, fiscal transfers, or additional financing may be required.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect investment planning with portfolios and pipelines
implementationGuidance.content: Use local budgets and investment plans to inform the development of coordinated climate portfolios and project pipelines (see Pathway 3.2)

implementationGuidance.title: Support monitoring and improvement
implementationGuidance.content: Encourage consistent reporting on climate-related budget allocations, expenditure, and results. Use findings to improve national guidance and municipal budgeting practices over time.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – CapaCITIES Program
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Launched in 2016 with Swiss funding, CapaCITIES supported cities in developing Net-Zero Climate Resilient City Action Plans, identifying priority investments and strengthening municipal capacities. The National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, partnered with the program to ensure alignment of methodologies with national standards, facilitate engagement with municipal governments, adapt program tools for national use and connect project learnings with national policies and programs. Across participating cities, the plans identified INR 7,142 billion (around USD 73 billion) in climate investment needs. A notable example is Tirunelveli city’s Net Zero Climate-Resilient Cities Action Plan, supported by NIUA under CapaCITIES, which identifies priority investments, indicative costs, potential financing sources and implementation responsibilities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: India shows how national institutions and development partners can support local climate investment planning and connect it with national programs.

illustrativeExamples.title: Philippines – Local Climate Change Expenditure Tagging
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Philippines institutionalized local climate expenditure tagging through joint national guidelines that linked climate priorities with local investment programs and annual budgets. In 2015, the Climate Change Commission (CCC), Department of Budget and Management (DBM), and Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) issued joint guidelines for tagging climate-related expenditure in local Annual Investment Programs (AIPs), which identify planned local projects, activities, costs and funding sources for annual budgeting. The guidelines introduced common climate expenditure classifications, revised investment program forms and reporting procedures. To support their adoption, the DBM incorporates tagging into local budget guidance, the CCC guides local governments in classifying climate-related expenditure and reviews the accuracy of these classifications. At the same time, the DILG facilitates implementation across local governments. Using these guidelines, provinces, cities, and municipalities identify climate-related allocations and funding sources through their AIPs and prepare investment briefs to support prioritization, expenditure monitoring, and identification of financing needs.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: The Philippines shows how national regulations, common methodologies, and technical support can integrate climate priorities into local investment planning and budgeting.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Stockholm's Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Stockholm incorporates climate targets and implementation responsibilities into its annual financial budget, with progress monitored through the city's management system. Municipal departments and companies can also access a dedicated climate investment fund to support priority measures. As part of its Climate City Contract (CCC) under the EU Cities Mission, Stockholm prepared a 2030 Climate Neutrality Investment Plan outlining how the city's transition could be financed, including investment responsibilities beyond the municipality. This planning takes place within Sweden's broader CCC process, coordinated through Viable Cities in partnership with national government agencies. The process provides a framework for national–local collaboration on climate priorities, investment needs and financing arrangements.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Stockholm shows how municipal climate budgeting and investment planning can connect with national–local coordination processes.

illustrativeExamples.title: C40 – Climate Budgeting Framework
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The C40 Climate Budgeting Framework (CBF) helps cities to establish climate budgeting processes that connect climate targets with annual or multiyear budget decisions. It covers operating and capital budgets, emphasizes leadership by municipal finance departments and coordination across departments and integrates implementation responsibilities, monitoring, and learning into regular budget cycles. C40's accompanying guidance highlights how cities can use climate budgets to engage national governments on financing priority climate investments. National governments can further support adoption through compatible public-finance regulations, common budgeting guidance, and technical assistance.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: This framework helps cities integrate climate priorities into their budgeting and identify opportunities for national support, including financing and enabling regulations.

illustrativeExamples.title: NDC Partnership and Green Climate Fund – Climate Investment Planning and Mobilization Framework
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by the NDC Partnership and Green Climate Fund, this framework guides governments through climate investment planning and finance mobilization. It helps to translate NDCs, adaptation plans, and long-term climate strategies into investment priorities and finance mobilization approaches. The framework recommends engaging subnational authorities, aligning national investment planning with existing subnational investment frameworks, and reviewing financing needs and gaps across government levels. It also supports incorporating existing subnational investment priorities and pipelines into country-level planning.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Structure national climate investment planning, including coordination among relevant government institutions and stakeholders.

illustrativeExamples.title: CDP – Adaptation and Action Explorer
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Adaptation and Action Explorer is an AI-powered platform that combines climate and nature hazard data with information reported by more than 1,000 cities, states and regions. It helps subnational governments assess physical climate risks, connect these with existing adaptation actions and projects, identify adaptation pathways, prioritise investments, and communicate their needs and readiness to funders and partners.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Understand local climate risks, identify adaptation priorities and strengthen the visibility of projects seeking finance.

pathways.title: 3.2 Climate Portfolios and Project Pipelines
pathways.overview: Climate portfolios bring together different projects and interventions around shared climate priorities. These may include infrastructure investments, policy and regulatory reforms, governance improvements, capacity building and other measures for implementation. By combining these interventions in a portfolio, governments can address governance and finance barriers that individual projects cannot resolve alone. As portfolios develop, suitable projects can be integrated into project pipelines for further preparation and financing. National governments can support this process by coordinating national and subnational investment priorities, facilitating access to project preparation support, and identifying opportunities to aggregate similar municipal projects into project pipelines. This can improve investment readiness and help attract financing for projects that may be difficult to finance individually.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Adapt portfolio development to institutional context. It may be led by national agencies, country platforms, subnational government associations, or municipal authorities.
Account for differences in local capacities. Cities with limited capacities may need additional technical support for pipeline development and aggregation.
Consider the maturity of project pipelines. Some cities may already have advanced pipelines, while others require support from concept identification.

implementationGuidance.title: Support portfolio development
implementationGuidance.content: Convene relevant national and subnational institutions to identify complementary projects and interventions around shared climate priorities. These may include infrastructure, policy, regulatory and capacity-building measures, with clear responsibilities and sequencing. Ensure that the portfolios remained aligned with NDC commitments (see Pathway 1.1).

implementationGuidance.title: Identify project pipelines
implementationGuidance.content: Assess which projects within portfolios have potential for further preparation and financing. Consider their climate impact, investment requirements, and current readiness.

implementationGuidance.title: Explore financing pathways
implementationGuidance.content: Identify projects requiring additional development finance or borrowing or having potential for private investment. Flag projects requiring further risk reduction (see Pathway 4.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Explore project aggregation
implementationGuidance.content: Where cities have similar investment needs, explore coordinated project pipelines or common investment programs to achieve scale and improve access to finance (see Pathway 4.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Establish portfolio coordination arrangements
implementationGuidance.content: Assign responsibility for maintaining portfolios, coordinating institutions and tracking progress across projects and other interventions (see Pathway 1.3).

illustrativeExamples.title: European Union – Mission for Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The EU Cities Mission supports 112 selected cities in developing Climate City Contracts through the NetZeroCities platform. These contracts include Climate Neutrality Action Plans that bring together infrastructure, policy, governance, and other interventions into coordinated portfolios. Cities also develop complementary Climate Neutrality Investment Plans that assess the capital needed to deliver these portfolios and identify potential public and private financing sources. The portfolio approach helps cities to move beyond individual projects and organize interventions around a shared climate mission, while involving local, regional, and national stakeholders.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: The EU Cities Mission shows how common frameworks, technical assistance, and multilevel collaboration can support cities in developing coordinated climate investment portfolios.

illustrativeExamples.title: Egypt – EBRD Green Cities Green City Action Plans
illustrativeExamples.fullText: EBRD Green Cities illustrates how multilateral development banks and national institutions can support cities in developing integrated portfolios of climate projects and policy interventions. Participating cities use Green City Action Plans to assess environmental challenges, identify priorities, and develop pipelines of infrastructure investments, along with policy reforms and institutional measures. The plans identify expected benefits and costs, financing options, and implementation responsibilities. The EBRD supports the process through technical assistance, policy dialogue and infrastructure financing. In Egypt, the Green City Action Plan for 6th of October City was developed with the involvement of the New Urban Communities Authority (NUCA), a national government authority, and the city administration. Together, they engaged stakeholders to identify environmental priorities and develop a coordinated portfolio.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: These plans show how development banks and national urban institutions can support city-level portfolio development, combining infrastructure investments with policy and institutional measures.

illustrativeExamples.title: Brazil – Green and Resilient Cities Programme (PCVR) Project Bank
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Brazil illustrates how a national program can identify and coordinate urban climate investment pipelines. Developed through a partnership involving the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change, CCFLA, and the University of Brasília, the PCVR Project Bank consolidates information on climate-related projects submitted by municipalities, states and public enterprises. The bank has received 733 project submissions, including 487 submitted by municipal governments. The projects that reported estimated costs together require approximately BRL 14.1 billion (USD 2.6 billion) in financing. By mapping projects across sectors and stages of development, the bank provides an overview of local investment needs and opportunities for project preparation. This can help development banks, technical assistance providers, and financing partners identify opportunities to support municipal investment pipelines in Brazil.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Brazil shows how national programs can consolidate municipal climate project proposals and identify investment needs.

pathways.title: 3.3 Project Preparation
pathways.overview: Project preparation is the process of developing climate action concepts into bankable projects that can secure financing from public or private sources. It can help develop a pipeline of bankable projects from investment opportunities in project portfolios. Project preparation typically involves four stages: concept development, pre-feasibility, feasibility, and financial structuring and transactions. These stages help assess technical, financial, environmental, social, and regulatory risks, and develop projects that meet financiers' requirements. However, cities often lack the technical expertise, institutional capacity and upfront resources for thorough project preparation. National governments can address these barriers by establishing or strengthening project preparation facilities, facilitating project aggregation, and connecting municipal project pipelines with multilateral or national development banks and other financing partners.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Build on existing institutions with project preparation mandates and expertise. National development banks, government agencies, or dedicated PPFs may provide support, depending on institutional arrangements.

Consider differences in capacities. Cities with limited technical and financial expertise may require more intensive support from early concept development. More capable municipalities may only need specialized assistance for feasibility studies, financial structuring, or transactions.

Ensure sustained funding for project preparation, recognizing that not all prepared projects will secure financing. Consider dedicated grants, revolving preparation funds, or development-partner support.

implementationGuidance.title: Strengthen subnational access to project preparation
implementationGuidance.content: Establish or strengthen national project preparation facilities (PPFs) or connect municipal pipelines with existing national and international PPFs. Provide funding and technical assistance where needed.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage financing partners early
implementationGuidance.content: Involve national development banks, multilateral development banks, climate funds and other potential financiers to understand their investment requirements. Use their inputs to guide urban and subnational project preparation.

implementationGuidance.title: Coordinate preparation support
implementationGuidance.content: Identify similar project preparation needs across municipalities. Explore shared technical assistance, standardized approaches, or pooled preparation resources to reduce preparation costs and improve efficiency. Leverage a country platform where available (see Pathway 1.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Track project preparation outcomes
implementationGuidance.content: Monitor progress from concept development through feasibility and financial structuring. Use findings to refine project pipelines and identify additional interventions or preparation needs. Address delays and connect sufficiently prepared projects with national and international financing opportunities (see Pathways 1.3, 3.2, 4.2).

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – DBSA Municipal Project Preparation
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) manages ZAR 50 million (around USD 3 million) in project preparation funding through the national Infrastructure Fund for six municipalities, including Vhembe, Ugu, and Sol Plaatje. The program supports water, sanitation, and electricity infrastructure projects through technical, financial, economic, environmental, and socioeconomic feasibility studies. DBSA also helps municipalities to utilize implementation models, structure project financing, and explore blended finance and private-sector participation. The program aims to develop bankable municipal infrastructure projects and attract public and private investment.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: South Africa’s national development bank pools project preparation resources and expertise to support municipal infrastructure investment.

illustrativeExamples.title: Indonesia – Project Development Facility, Regional Infrastructure Development Fund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Indonesia illustrates how a national development finance institution can support subnational governments in preparing infrastructure projects for investment. PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur (PT SMI), a state-owned institution under the Ministry of Finance, implemented the Regional Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), supported by the World Bank and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Alongside infrastructure lending, RIDF established a Project Development Facility to help subnational governments identify and prepare projects through feasibility studies, detailed engineering designs, environmental and social assessments, and procurement support. The facility was supported by a USD 3 million grant for technical assistance, complementing the fund's infrastructure lending. This helped address municipal project preparation gaps and connect local infrastructure proposals with financing opportunities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Indonesia shows how national development finance institutions can combine dedicated project preparation support with infrastructure lending to strengthen subnational investment pipelines.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA – Project Preparation Resource Directory
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Directory helps subnational governments and stakeholders identify project preparation facilities (PPFs) that can support them in developing green and resilient infrastructure, including implementing more efficient heating and cooling systems, building renewable energy, setting up sustainable transit, or climate-proofing resilient infrastructure. Users can filter information by region, country, sector, project stage, etc., to find PPFs for their project needs.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Identify suitable project preparation facilities that can provide technical and financial support for preparing urban climate projects.

illustrativeExamples.title: NDC Partnership – Project Preparation Support Database
illustrativeExamples.fullText: This searchable database of international, regional, national, and subnational project preparation facilities is focused on supporting the preparation of climate-aligned projects, as well as incubators and accelerators supporting climate-aligned businesses.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Find project preparation facilities and support programs that match climate investment priorities and project development needs.

illustrativeExamples.title: ICLEI and Gap Fund – Capacity Development Toolkit for Early-Stage Project Preparation
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The toolkit provides 12 practical tools and templates developed through the Gap Fund Step-Up Project with cities in Africa and South America. It helps city officials and technical partners assess technical capacity and data gaps, map stakeholders and risks, develop basic financial models, and evaluate financing options. Each tool includes practical guidance and adaptable templates to strengthen early-stage project preparation.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: A toolkit for strengthening municipal capacities to assess project feasibility, address preparation gaps, and improve investment readiness.

illustrativeExamples.title: Urban-Act – Early-Stage City Climate Project Bankability Diagnostic Tool
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The tool is designed to support cities during the early stages of project preparation, from concept to pre-feasibility by applying a project finance lens to improve project viability and financeability. It offers tailored checklists across six thematic investment areas to identify bankability gaps and finance-readiness issues, along with practical sector-specific recommendations to strengthen project design, financial viability, and access to climate finance.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Identify bankability gaps in early-stage climate projects and determine the technical and financial preparation needed to address them.

illustrativeExamples.title: SOURCE – Sustainable Infrastructure Project Preparation Platform
illustrativeExamples.fullText: SOURCE is a digital project preparation and management platform developed through a multilateral development bank initiative and coordinated by the Sustainable Infrastructure Foundation. It provides standardized, sector-specific templates to help governments define, prepare, and manage sustainable infrastructure projects throughout their lifecycle. Its features include project monitoring, document management, preparation guidance and tools for connecting projects with preparation facilities and potential financiers. SOURCE is used in more than 50 countries.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Standardize infrastructure project preparation across government institutions and improve project quality, transparency, and investment readiness.

conceptBoxes.title: What are Project Preparation Facilities?
conceptBoxes.excerpt: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing bankable, investment-ready projects, typically from a project’s concept, design, or scoping stage up to the financial close.
conceptBoxes.fullText: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing bankable, investment-ready projects, typically from a project’s concept, design, or scoping stage up to the financial close. A PPF may provide technical and/or financial support. PPFs can provide a wide range of support depending on a project’s stage and sector. The overarching goal of PPFs is preparing bankable, or investment-ready, projects. A project is bankable, whether from public or private sources, when its risk-return profile meets investors’ criteria. Key criteria include the probability of success, sufficient estimated cash flows to cover costs and produce returns that meet investor expectations, and whether the project will be implemented by a creditworthy entity.

formattedActions.title: Mobilize Finance and Shape Markets
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to work with cities, subnational governments, and financing partners to mobilize capital and strengthen markets for urban climate solutions. It covers local climate funds, financial instruments and mechanisms, and aggregation approaches that improve financing access, address investment risks, shape markets, and support implementation at scale.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Climate investment portfolios require financing arrangements suited to their needs and risks. Local climate funds can mobilize and channel resources toward priority investments, while financial instruments and mechanisms can help to improve financing terms and manage risks. Aggregation can achieve scale by pooling financing needs, risks, or purchasing demand, strengthening access to capital and markets for climate solutions. These approaches can complement one another.

pathways.title: 4.1 Local Climate Funds
pathways.overview: Local climate funds mobilize and channel financial resources toward locally identified climate investments. They can draw on municipal budgets, national transfers, international grants, philanthropic contributions, and private capital, depending on their design. Funds may take different forms, including municipal, community-based or devolved climate funds and can support investments that are difficult to finance through conventional municipal budgets or commercial sources alone. National governments can enable local climate funds through supportive legal and fiscal frameworks, funding, and partnerships with financial institutions.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Consider the types of investments local funds need to support. Grant-based arrangements may suit adaptation and public-good projects, often without revenue streams, while repayable finance may be appropriate for revenue-generating projects.

Consider differences in local access to finance. Where municipalities face borrowing restrictions or limited access to financial markets, local funds may rely more heavily on fiscal transfers, grants, or financing channelled through national institutions.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify local financing needs and investment gaps
implementationGuidance.content: Start from city investment plans and portfolios. Assess project ownership, readiness, financing needs, and potential revenue sources (see Pathways 3.1 and 3.2).

relatedPathways.title: 3.1 Local Climate Budgeting and Investment Planning

implementationGuidance.title: Support the establishment of local climate funds
implementationGuidance.content: Help local or subnational governments to establish suitable fund arrangements, considering enabling legal frameworks, fiscal responsibilities, and institutional capacities (see Pathway 2.2).

relatedPathways.title: 2.2 Reform Roadmaps for Urban Climate Investment

implementationGuidance.title: Clarify governance arrangements
implementationGuidance.content: Agree on responsibilities for fund management, resource allocation, and oversight. Ensure local governments retain ownership of investment priorities, with national oversight where appropriate.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilize sustained finance
implementationGuidance.content: Connect funds with long-term national funding programs, fiscal transfers, and development partners. Facilitate contributions from philanthropic organizations, businesses, and other financing partners, including through country platforms where relevant (see Pathway 1.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Strengthen fund management
implementationGuidance.content: Facilitate cities’ access to financial management and investment appraisal expertise. Establish reporting and monitoring arrangements to track resource allocation, investment outcomes, and fund performance.

illustrativeExamples.title: Kenya – County Climate Change Funds
illustrativeExamples.fullText: First piloted in Isiolo in 2011–12, County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs) enable Kenyan counties to identify, prioritize, and finance local adaptation projects through county planning and budgeting systems. County and ward committees guide investment decisions, drawing on local knowledge and climate information. Several counties have committed 1–2% of their development budgets to these funds. These commitments helped to attract external finance, including seed funding from the UK and Sweden. CCCFs are aligned with Kenya’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP), the National Climate Change Action Plan, and the Climate Change Act. The success of pilots helped to pave the way for national scale-up. By 2023, all 47 Kenyan counties had CCCFs in place, creating the basis for a new Financing Locally Led Climate Action Program funded by the World Bank and the governments of Denmark and Sweden, and led by the National Treasury.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Kenya shows how national governments can scale locally led climate finance through devolved funding arrangements that include local decision-making and combine domestic resources with international climate finance.

illustrativeExamples.title: Italy – ForestaMi Fund, Milan
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Launched in 2019, Forestami brings together the Municipality and Metropolitan City of Milan, Lombardy Region, universities, foundations and other local institutions to support urban forestry and climate resilience. A local fund was established within Fondazione di Comunità Milano to mobilize contributions from businesses and citizens toward the goal of planting three million trees by 2030. In April 2025, the initiative transitioned into Fondazione Forestami, an independent nonprofit foundation responsible for expanding its activities across the metropolitan area and beyond.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Milan shows how municipal and regional governments can partner with philanthropic institutions and businesses to mobilize dedicated funding for local climate action.

illustrativeExamples.title: UK – Bristol's Local Climate Investment Funds
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Through its Climate Action Investment initiative, developed under the EU NetZeroCities Pilot Cities Programme, Bristol City Council enables residents and businesses to invest as little as GBP 5 in energy-efficiency and renewable-energy improvements to council-owned buildings. The initiative raised over GBP 500,000 in its first five weeks toward an initial GBP 1 million target, offering investors a five-year loan with 4.2% annual interest. Separately, the Bristol City Leap Community Energy Fund provides GBP 1.5 million in grants and loans for community-led energy projects, funded equally by private partners Ameresco and Vattenfall. The Bristol City Leap model also informed the UK government's Local Net Zero Accelerator program, which supported a pilot in York and North Yorkshire to explore replicating its approach to mobilizing private investment for local net-zero projects.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Bristol shows how cities can mobilize community and private capital through local funds, and how national governments can support the replication of successful models.

illustrativeExamples.title: Bhutan – Local Climate Adaptive Living Facility (LoCAL)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Introduced in 2011 through a partnership between the Royal Government of Bhutan and UNCDF, LoCAL uses performance-based climate resilience grants and technical assistance to finance locally identified adaptation investments. The program expanded to over 100 local governments, financing more than 350 adaptation investments by 2023. Building on this experience, Bhutan has integrated LoCAL into its national local government financing system and planned to mobilize domestic resources through the same grant mechanism. This would allow the government to sustain and expand local adaptation financing beyond the initial international support. Accordingly, Bhutan has incorporated performance-based grants into its central budgeting system and included climate vulnerability in the formula for allocating resources to local governments.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Bhutan shows how national governments can use existing fiscal transfer systems to channel climate finance to local authorities and strengthen domestic financing arrangements.

illustrativeExamples.title: Viable Cities – Local Investment Structures – design considerations
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed through Viable Cities and the Viability Fund for Cities, this working model is intended for local governments, investment owners, country platforms and finance partners. It describes common functions for coordinating a local investment portfolio, identifying owners and preparation needs, matching investments with suitable capital and supporting implementation and reinvestment. Institutional arrangements can vary with local mandates, revenue models and legal conditions. National coordination can connect several local portfolios with larger programmes and domestic and international finance, complemented where appropriate by philanthropic and private capital. The model supports the CHAMP Implementation Roadmap 2026–2028 and identifies questions requiring further validation.
