illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Develop locally anchored investment arrangements when several owners and capital providers need to coordinate preparation, financing and implementation of a climate transition portfolio.

pathways.title: 4.2 Financial Instruments and Mechanisms
pathways.overview: National governments can work with development banks and financing partners to deploy financial instruments and mechanisms that help cities access capital for climate projects. These include concessional loans, guarantees, insurance, green bonds, and other risk-sharing mechanisms that address specific financing barriers. Public and concessional resources can also be combined with commercial finance through blended finance arrangements to mobilize additional investment. The choice of instruments depends on project financing needs, risks, local market conditions, and municipal financial capacities.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Consider municipal borrowing powers and financial regulations when selecting instruments. Where direct borrowing or bond issuance is restricted, national institutions may need to channel financing through intermediaries, such as utilities, public enterprises or public banks.

Consider differences in municipal creditworthiness and financial management capacities. Cities with limited financial capacity may require concessional finance, credit enhancement, or additional support before accessing commercial instruments.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify project financing needs and risk profiles
implementationGuidance.content: Work with cities, development banks and financing partners to assess project revenue streams, creditworthiness, and financing barriers across municipal pipelines (see Pathways 2.1 and 3.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Select appropriate financial instruments
implementationGuidance.content: Match financial mechanisms to project requirements and municipal financial capacities. Use concessional loans for projects with limited revenue potential, guarantees to address credit risks, and green bonds or commercial debt for revenue-generating infrastructure.

implementationGuidance.title: Deploy risk mitigation and blended finance
implementationGuidance.content: Engage national development banks, multilateral institutions and international climate funds to provide guarantees, insurance, and other risk mitigation mechanisms. Where appropriate, use national public finance to help mobilize private investment, as part of a blended finance approach.

implementationGuidance.title: Monitor financing outcomes
implementationGuidance.content: Track financing mobilized, financing costs, risk reduction, and investment outcomes. Use findings to improve the effectiveness of financial instruments over time.

illustrativeExamples.title: Nigeria – InfraCredit
illustrativeExamples.fullText: InfraCredit was established in 2017 through a partnership between the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority and the Private Infrastructure Development Group's GuarantCo. It provides local currency guarantees that improve the credit quality of infrastructure bonds and attract long-term investment from domestic pension funds, insurers, and banks. By the end of 2024, it had guaranteed 24 transactions, mobilizing over NGN 200 billion in private investment and supporting nearly NGN 150 billion in bond issuances. These include North South Power's NGN 8.5 billion green bond, Nigeria's first certified corporate green bond. Its approach has informed similar credit-enhancement facilities in Pakistan and Kenya, demonstrating how nationally supported guarantees can expand domestic infrastructure financing.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Nigeria shows how national institutions can partner with development finance organizations to reduce credit risks and mobilize long-term domestic capital for climate-related infrastructure.

illustrativeExamples.title: Brazil – BNDES Climate Fund (Fundo Clima)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Fundo Clima provides climate financing on preferential terms to municipalities, including extended repayment and grace periods. It is coordinated by the Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change and operated by the national development bank BNDES. In May 2026, BNDES announced BRL 500 million in financing for Belo Horizonte's municipal climate-resilience investment plan, including BRL 480 million from Fundo Clima. The financing will support flood and landslide prevention, green infrastructure, and restoration of rivers and water sources.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Brazil shows how national governments can leverage national development banks to provide preferential, long-term financing for municipal climate investments.

illustrativeExamples.title: Greece – EIB Sustainable Urban Development Framework Loans
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Framework loans from the European Investment Bank (EIB) provide long-term financing for multiple smaller projects under multiyear investment programs, allowing eligible investments to be financed over time without requiring separate loans for each project. In Greece, the EIB signed EUR 1 billion (around USD 1.1 billion) in framework loans to support the Antonis Tritsis national public investment program, led by the Ministry of Interior. Financing in the program is channeled through the Consignment Deposits and Loans Fund for municipal investments in flood protection, sustainable water and waste management, energy-efficient public buildings, and e-mobility.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Greece shows how national ministries can work with multilateral development banks to finance smaller municipal climate projects through flexible, long-term financing arrangements.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA – Financial Instruments Toolkit
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Financial Instruments Toolkit is an interactive resource that helps practitioners explore financial instruments for urban climate projects, including how different instruments work and the contexts in which they may be relevant. It provides structured guidance on navigating the spectrum of urban climate finance instruments—from debt, equity, and guarantees to results-based financing and blended capital structures—helping project developers and municipal leaders match the right financial mechanisms to their specific infrastructure and resilience needs.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Identify financial instruments suited to specific urban climate investment needs, financing barriers and local market conditions.

illustrativeExamples.title: ICLEI – Climate Finance Decision-Making Tree
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by ICLEI, this tool guides local and regional governments through a series of questions to identify suitable financing options for climate investments. It considers factors such as available municipal resources and assets, borrowing eligibility, project revenue potential, private-sector participation and access to public funding. The decision tree covers financing options including grants, loans, municipal green bonds, public-private partnerships, blended finance and risk mitigation instruments. Each option is accompanied by guidance on its advantages, limitations and relevant case studies, helping governments compare potential financing approaches. National governments can also use the tool to understand municipal financing constraints and identify where public financing, guarantees or regulatory support may be needed to expand access to financing.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Compare financing options and identify instruments appropriate to local government capacities, investment requirements, and financing conditions.

conceptBoxes.title: What is Blended Finance?
conceptBoxes.excerpt: Blended finance is the strategic use of a limited amount of concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize additional finance, primarily from commercial and private sources — toward sustainable development and climate goals.
conceptBoxes.fullText: Blended finance is the strategic use of a limited amount of concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize additional finance, primarily from commercial and private sources — toward sustainable development and climate goals. Rather than a single financial instrument, it is a structuring approach: public actors (donors, development agencies, philanthropies, and development finance institutions) absorb or share risks that would otherwise deter private investors, improving a project's risk-return profile enough to attract market-rate capital. The concessional capital at the core of a blended structure can take several forms, including grants, concessional debt or equity, guarantees, and other risk-sharing facilities. These de-risking mechanisms matter most in emerging markets and developing economies, where country-specific risk accounts for between 60 and 90 percent of investors' risk considerations, and where about 80–90 percent of climate mitigation investment is expected to come from the private sector. The overarching goal is to crowd in private money that would not have been invested otherwise, deploying only as much public subsidy as is needed to make a project viable.

pathways.title: 4.3 Financial Aggregation and Market Shaping
pathways.overview: Financial aggregation helps cities and other actors combine financial resources or coordinate demand to improve access to finance, reduce costs, and strengthen markets for climate solutions. On the supply side, it can involve pooling capital from multiple financiers. On the demand side, it can involve aggregating municipal borrowing needs, pooling insurance risks, or coordinating public and private purchasing demand. These approaches can improve access to finance, reduce costs, and shape markets by creating larger investment opportunities, strengthening insurance markets, or signaling demand for low-carbon solutions. National governments can support aggregation through enabling regulations, pooled financing and insurance facilities, national development banks, and coordinated procurement programs.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Consider the scale and similarity of financing or purchasing needs. Aggregation may offer limited benefits where participation from cities is low or borrowing, insurance, and purchasing requirements differ substantially across municipalities.

Consider existing institutional mandates and capacities. National agencies, municipal financial intermediaries, or intermunicipal partnerships may manage aggregation, depending on their legal authority and ability to coordinate participants.

Account for differences in financial and supplier markets. Where domestic lenders, insurers or low-carbon suppliers are limited, national governments may need to engage international partners or provide credit enhancement for pooled borrowing.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify opportunities for aggregation
implementationGuidance.content: Work with cities, financing institutions, and partners to identify common borrowing, insurance, or purchasing needs, including those emerging from municipal portfolios and pipelines. Assess whether aggregation could improve financing access, reduce costs, or strengthen demand for climate solutions (see Pathway 3.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Select suitable aggregation approaches
implementationGuidance.content: Explore pooled financing facilities, joint borrowing arrangements, collective insurance or coordinated purchasing, depending on local needs and market conditions. Clarify participating institutions, responsibilities, and financing or purchasing commitments.

implementationGuidance.title: Establish supportive enabling arrangements
implementationGuidance.content: Provide clear legal frameworks, standardized procedures, and technical assistance to support aggregation. Where needed, establish credit-enhancement mechanisms or guarantee facilities to lower borrowing costs for pooled financing (see Pathway 2.2).

relatedPathways.title: 2.2 Reform Roadmaps for Urban Climate Investment

implementationGuidance.title: Engage market actors
implementationGuidance.content: Work with institutional investors, commercial lenders, insurers, manufacturers, and solution providers to communicate aggregated demand, establish common specifications, and structure investment or procurement opportunities.

implementationGuidance.title: Manage implementation and scale
implementationGuidance.content: Monitor implementation, evaluate cost savings and risk reduction, and refine aggregation models. Use successful pilots to expand participation across cities and sectors over time.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – Tamil Nadu Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India illustrates how state and national governments can use credit enhancement to help smaller municipalities access long-term infrastructure finance. Established by the Government of Tamil Nadu in 2002, the Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund pooled the borrowing needs of 13 municipalities and issued a USD 6.2 million bond for water and sanitation investments. To reduce investor risks, the state government established reserve funds and escrow accounts to intercept fiscal transfers if repayments fell short, while a USAID partial guarantee provided additional protection. This blended finance arrangement helped to secure an AA credit rating and 15-year financing for municipalities that would otherwise struggle to access capital markets independently. Building on pooled financing experiences in Tamil Nadu and other states, India's national government established the Pooled Finance Development Fund in 2006 to support state-level financing entities through credit enhancement and project preparation assistance.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: India shows how state and national governments can use blended finance, guarantees and credit enhancement to improve smaller municipalities' access to long-term infrastructure finance

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Kommuninvest
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Kommuninvest is a municipally owned financial institution that raises capital from financial markets and lends to its municipal and regional members. Backed by joint guarantees from 282 municipalities and 15 regions in Sweden, it aggregates borrowing needs to improve access to capital and reduce financing costs for local infrastructure, including climate-related investments. In 2025, its total lending reached SEK 563.9 billion (approximately USD 56.8 billion), demonstrating the scale of pooled municipal financing. Sweden's legal framework for municipal borrowing enables this model, while the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority provides regulatory oversight. While Kommuninvest provides long-term debt financing, there are avenues to enhance its offerings to municipalities in the form of early-stage project preparation, risk capital or coordination of climate investment portfolios.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Sweden shows how national legal and regulatory frameworks can enable municipalities to jointly establish financial institutions that pool borrowing needs and improve access to long-term capital.

illustrativeExamples.title: Argentina – RAMCC Trust Fund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Established in 2018 by the Argentine Network of Municipalities against Climate Change (RAMCC), the Trust Fund enables participating municipalities to pool resources and collectively procure climate-smart technologies. Its governance includes an Assembly of Mayors representing participating municipalities, an elected executive committee, and a technical secretariat supporting project development and financing. The fund has supported joint procurement of LED streetlighting, helping municipalities to achieve economies of scale, reduce procurement costs, and improve energy efficiency. The model demonstrates how intermunicipal cooperation can strengthen purchasing power and support implementation of local climate action plans.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Argentina’s intermunicipal aggregation mechanism helps to establish shared financing and procurement to aggregate demand, reduce costs, and implement climate investments.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – Grand Challenge for Electric Buses
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Led by Convergence Energy Services Limited (CESL), a subsidiary of the Ministry of Power's Energy Efficiency Services Limited, the Grand Challenge pooled demand for electric buses across multiple cities through a single procurement process. CESL worked with participating cities to assess fleet requirements, routes and charging infrastructure, while engaging manufacturers to develop standardized tender specifications. Supported by national subsidies and some state contributions, the program used gross-cost contracts under which private operators finance, own and operate buses and charging infrastructure for 12 years, reducing upfront capital requirements for municipalities. This approach helped to achieve economies of scale, lower procurement costs and support wider adoption of electric buses.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: India shows how national institutions can aggregate municipal purchasing demand and coordinate procurement to reduce costs and accelerate low-carbon transport deployment.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Philippines – City Disaster Insurance Pool (PCDIP)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed under the leadership of the Department of Finance with technical assistance from the Asian Development Bank, the Philippine City Disaster Insurance Pool aims to provide affordable parametric insurance against typhoons and earthquakes. Ten cities were identified and agreed to participate in the design process, which included disaster exposure mapping and capacity building. The proposed model will pool municipal insurance demand through the Government Service Insurance System and transfer risks to domestic and international reinsurance markets. This arrangement is expected to reduce insurance costs and provide payouts within 15 business days of qualifying disasters to support early recovery.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: The Philippines shows how national governments can design insurance arrangements to pool municipal disaster risks and improve cities’ access to climate-risk protection.

illustrativeExamples.title: Viability Fund for Cities – Aggregated Purchasing Power Framework
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Published by the Viability Fund for Cities and drawing on Viable Cities’ work with cities and partners, this framework helps local governments, public and private buyers, country platforms and finance partners coordinate demand for low-carbon solutions across construction, retrofitting, energy, logistics and other locally relevant purchasing areas. It explains how to make purchasing needs, budgets and timing visible, engage suppliers and use demonstrator evidence to inform procurement. Buyers retain their own budgets, contracts and decision rights, while shared requirements and credible demand signals can strengthen investment cases. The framework connects local purchasing opportunities with wider markets and investment portfolios, including through First Mover Cities, supporting the CHAMP Implementation Roadmap 2026–2028.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Coordinate public and private purchasing when fragmented demand limits market confidence and the investment needed to scale low-carbon solutions.

illustrativeExamples.title: CCFLA – Financial Aggregation Blueprints for Urban Climate Infrastructure
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by CCFLA, this report provides practical guidance through eight blueprints covering three types of financial aggregation: municipal pooled procurement, municipal green bonds and municipal insurance pooling. Drawing on examples from different geographies and institutional contexts, it examines how these instruments can be structured and implemented, including their benefits, challenges and enabling conditions.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Explore how cities can bundle smaller investment needs or investors to achieve economies of scale, reduce costs and improve access to finance for urban climate infrastructure.

formattedActions.title: Learn, Strengthen Capacities and Scale Implementation
formattedActions.description: This Action helps national governments to strengthen institutional capacities, learn from implementation, and support the scaling of urban climate investments through national and international partnerships. It covers systematic capacity building, real-world experimentation through System Demonstrators and international networks that facilitate knowledge exchange, access to expertise, financing partnerships, and implementation of effective approaches at scale.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Sustained climate investment requires local capacities that improve through practical experience and learning. Institutional capacity building helps municipal institutions to plan, finance, and implement climate projects, while system demonstrators provide them with opportunities to apply and strengthen capabilities through real-world experimentation. Learnings from implementation can inform future investment decisions, institutional practices and policy improvements. International networks help to cross-pollinate these learnings across cities, connect governments with expertise and financing partners, and support the adaptation and scaling of effective climate finance and implementation approaches.

pathways.title: 5.1 Institutional Capacity Building
pathways.overview: Cities and subnational governments often lack the institutional capacities needed to plan, finance and implement climate investments consistently. While project-specific technical assistance can address immediate gaps, systematic capacity building strengthens the skills, processes, and institutional knowledge needed for sustained investment. National governments can establish institutional capacity development programs, working with training institutions, development banks and other partners to address common municipal needs. These programs can help cities to apply new skills, strengthen internal systems and reduce dependence on external technical assistance.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Consider existing institutional arrangements and expertise when designing national programs. Training may be delivered through government institutions, development banks, universities or specialist partners, depending on their mandates and capacities.

Ensure programs are accessible to municipalities with different capacities and resources. Consider local languages, practical training formats, and additional support for smaller cities with limited staff and funding.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify institutional capacity gaps
implementationGuidance.content: Work with cities to assess recurring gaps in investment planning, financial management, project preparation, and implementation. Identify priorities for sustained capacity development across municipalities (see Pathway 2.1).

implementationGuidance.title: Develop capacity building programs
implementationGuidance.content: Develop training, mentoring, and institutional development programs around identified needs. Include practical skills in climate action and investment planning, financial instruments, business models, and infrastructure delivery.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilize training partners
implementationGuidance.content: Engage national development banks, universities, training institutions, and development partners to deliver programs. Build on existing national training systems where possible (see Pathway 5.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Connect learning with practical application
implementationGuidance.content: Link capacity-building activities to ongoing municipal investment priorities and projects. Use workshops, exercises, and hands-on support to help officials apply new skills.

implementationGuidance.title: Institutionalize capacities and track progress
implementationGuidance.content: Embed acquired skills into municipal processes, guidance, and staff development programs. Monitor improvements in financial management, investment readiness, and implementation capabilities.

illustrativeExamples.title: South Africa – DBSA Municipal Capacity Development Programme
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) illustrates how a national development bank can partner with the private sector to strengthen municipal technical and financial capacities. The DBSA, in partnership with Anglo American, implemented a three-year program across municipalities, investing over ZAR 120 million to train 500 municipal officials and support the development of 26 infrastructure master plans. The program included hands-on training with support for infrastructure planning, revenue collection, financial management, and service delivery. Participating municipalities achieved an average 11.6% improvement in revenue collection.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: South Africa shows how a national development bank can partner with the private sector to strengthen municipal financial management and infrastructure delivery capabilities.

illustrativeExamples.title: Morocco – Climate Change Competence Centre
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Climate Change Competence Centre of Morocco (4C Maroc) supports training and knowledge exchange across national and local governments, businesses, civil society, and research institutions. The platform has trained over 800 local actors, working with more than 15 national ministries, public institutions, and associations representing regional and local governments. Its activities strengthen capacities to integrate climate priorities into subnational planning and improve local access to climate finance.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Morocco shows how a national institution can provide capacity development support for local climate finance and implementation.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sierra Leone – UrbanShift Climate Finance Capacity Building
illustrativeExamples.fullText: UrbanShift, a Global Environment Facility-funded program (concluded in 2025), provided systematic capacity-building support to strengthen urban climate investment capabilities. In Sierra Leone, the Ministry of Finance coordinated UrbanShift activities with Freetown City Council and identified government officials for training. Following participation in a Climate Finance City Academy in 2024, ministry officials recognized gaps in their draft fiscal decentralization policy and incorporated climate considerations into its implementation planning. UrbanShift also facilitated a peer exchange involving national and municipal officials to explore a proposed cable-car transport system for Freetown. This helped secure technical assistance from the C40 Cities Finance Facility for a feasibility study, demonstrating how capacity building and national–local collaboration can support municipal investment preparation.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Sierra Leone shows how national governments can leverage international capacity-building programs to strengthen climate finance policies and support municipal access to investment preparation.

illustrativeExamples.title: India – City Investments to Innovate, Integrate and Sustain (CITIIS 2.0)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: India’s national City Investments to Innovate, Integrate and Sustain (CITIIS 2.0) program can support municipal climate project implementation through financing, technical assistance, and institutional oversight. Led by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs in partnership with NIUA, AFD, KfW and the European Union, CITIIS 2.0 supports up to 18 competitively selected city projects focused on circular economy and integrated waste management. A national Project Management Unit at NIUA coordinates program delivery, monitoring, and technical support. Selected cities receive assistance from domestic experts and international mentors on project management, environmental and social safeguards, and implementation challenges.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: CITIIS 2.0 shows how national governments can combine financing, technical assistance, and institutional oversight to support the implementation of municipal climate projects.

illustrativeExamples.title: C40 Cities Finance Facility – City Academy on Finance and Equity (CAFE) Workbook
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by the C40 Cities Finance Facility, the CAFE workbook provides practical exercises to help city officials in developing countries enhance their understanding of climate finance instruments, assess project business models and integrate equity considerations into infrastructure investment decisions. The workbook contains case studies, knowledge, and tools to support municipal finance and planning teams in applying these concepts to their projects and programs.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Why use this tool: Support practical training on climate financing options, project business models and equitable investment planning.

pathways.title: 5.2 System Demonstrators
pathways.overview: System Demonstrators are real-world initiatives that test how multiple interconnected interventions across infrastructure, policy, governance, procurement, and capacity development can work together in practice to deliver urban climate transitions. They help cities and national governments identify and address practical implementation barriers, refine institutional and financial arrangements, and test new business models and procurement approaches in real-world contexts. Learnings from system demonstrators can inform policy and regulatory improvements, build institutional confidence, and create opportunities for investment and scaling.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Define the scope and boundaries of the system demonstrator according to local priorities and capabilities. A demonstrator may focus on a specific sector, neighbourhood, or city-wide transition, provided it addresses interconnected interventions and governance arrangements.

Align governance and funding arrangements to support experimentation. Ensure participating institutions have the mandate and flexibility to test new approaches, adapt interventions based on early findings, and share learnings.

Plan for evaluation and scaling from the outset. Design evaluation frameworks that capture governance, regulatory, and market learnings alongside technical and financial outcomes, ensuring findings inform national policy, institutional practices, and future investment decisions.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify system demonstrator opportunities
implementationGuidance.content: Identify urban systems or transition challenges where interconnected interventions are required to achieve climate goals. Select demonstration sites and sectors based on city commitment, strategic importance and potential for learning and scale (see Pathways 1.1 and 3.2).

implementationGuidance.title: Support locally led system demonstrators
implementationGuidance.content: Enable cities and local partners to define implementation portfolios, governance arrangements, and partnership structures. Provide grant funding, technical assistance, and national-level facilitation to support orchestration and execution.

implementationGuidance.title: Engage actors responsible for implementation
implementationGuidance.content: Bring together relevant government agencies, utilities, businesses, financiers, communities and other implementation partners. Clarify their roles, contributions and responsibilities for delivering different interventions within the portfolio.

implementationGuidance.title: Test financial, regulatory and market innovations
implementationGuidance.content: Use system demonstrators to test new business models, financial instruments, procurement approaches and regulatory adaptations in real-world contexts. Identify institutional and regulatory barriers that require national-level resolution (see Pathways 2.2, 4.2 and 4.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Establish shared evaluation and learning frameworks
implementationGuidance.content: Track implementation progress, system-wide impacts, and practical learnings across interventions. Use iterative planning and evaluation cycles to adjust activities and capture insights for national policies and programs.

implementationGuidance.title: Connect learning with policy, investment and scaling
implementationGuidance.content: Use evidence from system demonstrators to inform policy, regulatory, and procurement reforms, refine investment planning, and connect prepared project portfolios with national funding and development finance partners (see Pathways 1.3 and 3.2).

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – CoAction Lund
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CoAction Lund, supported through Sweden’s System Demonstrator program, brings together 36 organizations, including infrastructure providers, employers, property owners, universities and solution providers, around more than 40 activities in energy and mobility in Brunnshög, Lund. Led by Lund municipality, the demonstrator tests solutions alongside changes in governance, behavior and business models. CoAction Lund’s funding was kept flexible to allow for resources to shift toward promising solutions, such as EnergyNet – a decentralized electricity network enabling buildings and local energy resources to share renewable electricity. Testing EnergyNet has helped identify regulatory and market barriers related to grid codes, data sharing, and local energy markets, informing its further development and potential expansion. CoAction Lund also uses a shared evaluation framework to track progress across interventions and assess their wider effects on the urban system, helping partners to refine their approaches and share lessons for future implementation.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Sweden shows how nationally funded system demonstrators can help cities to test interconnected climate interventions, identify implementation barriers, and evaluate outcomes.

illustrativeExamples.title: United Kingdom – Bristol Thriving Places
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Bristol Thriving Places addressed the challenge of delivering affordable, zero-carbon housing on small brownfield sites previously considered unviable. Bristol City Council and the Bristol Housing Festival worked with a consortium led by social housing developer EDAROTH, alongside housing associations, infrastructure providers, government agencies, and research partners. The demonstrator developed an integrated approach involving housing delivery, financial appraisal, regulatory analysis and digital modeling. By aggregating small council-owned sites into one program, Bristol created sufficient scale for development, prompted a review of the council's treasury strategy and secured a development agreement of approximately GBP 10 million (around USD 13 million) through an existing national procurement framework. The approach subsequently informed the UK government's Small Sites Aggregator program, which aims to enable the contruction of 10,000 social rent homes annually.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Bristol shows how system demonstrators can test new financial appraisal and procurement approaches to overcome infrastructure delivery barriers and inform national programs.

illustrativeExamples.title: Sweden – Stockholm STOLT
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Supported through Sweden's national system demonstrator program, STOLT advances Stockholm's ambition for an emission-free inner city by 2030. It brings together municipal departments, businesses, researchers, and civil society around interventions including environmental zones, fossil-free transport procurement, electrified construction and off-peak logistics. The demonstrator addresses challenges such as limited municipal enforcement powers and the absence of electrification requirements in construction procurement and investment appraisal. Through quarterly planning, evaluation, and adjustment cycles, participating actors test approaches, address implementation barriers, and generate learning to improve procurement practices and inform transport-system transformation.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Stockholm shows how nationally supported system demonstrators can identify regulatory and procurement barriers, test implementation approaches, and inform future investment decisions.

illustrativeExamples.title: Uganda – Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed through the Climate Smart Cities Challenge, Green Community Cities brought together Makindye Ssabagabo municipality, UN-Habitat, Viable Cities, and an international consortium to address affordable, low-carbon housing as part of a wider urban system. Its proposed portfolio integrated modular and incremental housing, recycled building materials, renewable energy, waste management, water-saving technologies, and local employment. To make housing delivery financially viable and affordable, it also explored a public-private partnership involving municipal support, private landowners, developers, housing cooperatives and investors, alongside concessional finance and affordable housing loans. The initiative has secured approximately USD 380,000 in grant funding, established a recycling operation processing 62 tonnes of plastic monthly and created over 70 jobs. However, the experience also highlighted challenges in translating internationally developed solutions into local implementation, particularly where local institutional relationships and national–local coordination were weaker.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: Makindye Ssabagabo highlights the importance of locally anchored partnerships and institutional capacity for accessing finance, and implementing and scaling system demonstrators.

illustrativeExamples.title: Viable Cities and Dark Matter Labs – A blueprint for designing and funding urban system demonstrator programmes
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by Viable Cities and Dark Matter Labs, with contributions from CCFLA, Nesta, UNEP, UN-Habitat, the World Economic Forum and WRI, the blueprint is a guide for funders, national governments, city networks and international organisations designing system demonstrator programmes. A system demonstrator is a portfolio of mutually reinforcing interventions in a defined urban system, designed with the actors who have the mandate to change it. Drawing on Sweden’s system demonstrator programme and the Climate Smart Cities Challenge, the blueprint presents the method, three city cases, a programme model that works as a checklist for a concept note, sample selection criteria and a readiness ladder. For multilevel climate finance, it shows how to anchor demonstrators in national frameworks such as CHAMP-aligned country platforms, separate grant funding for orchestration from capital for implementation, connect portfolios to local climate investment structures and use aggregated demand to create credible markets.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Useful for anyone setting up a system demonstrator programme, from defining the mission and selecting cities to preparing portfolios for investment and procurement.

pathways.title: 5.3 International Networks and Partnerships
pathways.overview: International networks and partnerships can help national and subnational governments access specialized expertise, financing partners and opportunities for collaboration on urban climate investment. They enable governments to exchange practical experience, address shared investment challenges and develop partnerships that support financing, implementation and scaling. National governments can facilitate cities' participation in relevant international initiatives and help to translate these connections into technical assistance and financing opportunities.
pathways.transferabilityTitle: Adapting this pathway to your context
transferability: Prioritize international initiatives according to national and subnational investment needs. Initiatives may differ in their focus and support, from peer learning and capacity building to financing and implementation partnerships.

Consider participation barriers for smaller cities – these may lack the staff, funding, or international connections to engage in global networks. National governments can facilitate introductions, fund participation, or work through city networks to broaden access via local events and forums.

Account for the duration and continuity of international initiatives. International programs may be time-bound or evolve over time. Lasting benefits depend on whether knowledge, relationships, and capacities are retained within domestic institutions.

implementationGuidance.title: Identify opportunities for international engagement
implementationGuidance.content: Assess where cities could benefit from international expertise, financing partnerships, or collective action on shared climate investment challenges. Identify relevant networks, initiatives and global policy forums, such as the Ministerial Meeting on Urbanization and Climate Change at UNFCCC COPs, where subnational perspectives can inform international discussions and partnerships.

implementationGuidance.title: Facilitate city participation
implementationGuidance.content: Help cities navigate international programs, eligibility requirements, and partnership opportunities. Work with city associations or intermediaries to broaden participation, particularly where smaller municipalities lack resources or international connections.

implementationGuidance.title: Mobilize finance partners
implementationGuidance.content: Engage international organizations, development banks, climate funds, and private-sector partners around shared national and subnational investment priorities, including through country platforms where relevant. Explore opportunities for technical assistance, financing, and coordinated implementation support (see Pathway 1.3).

implementationGuidance.title: Track engagement outcomes
implementationGuidance.content: Monitor financing opportunities or implementation support emerging from international engagement. Integrate learning, expertise, and relationships into national and subnational institutions and capacity-building programs to sustain benefits beyond individual initiatives (see Pathway 5.1).

illustrativeExamples.title: Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance (CCFLA)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: CCFA brings together national governments, development partners, city networks, financial institutions, organizations, and technical experts to address barriers to urban climate investment. Through thematic Action Groups, members exchange practical experience on project preparation, adaptation finance, enabling environments, private finance, and other emerging challenges. These groups provide opportunities to connect actors across government levels and the climate finance ecosystem, identify common investment barriers, and develop collaborative responses. CCFLA also supports local and regional engagement through its Local Hubs (see Action 1), helping to connect international expertise with local climate finance priorities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: CCFLA shows how international networks can connect national and subnational governments with specialized climate finance expertise and opportunities for collaboration.

illustrativeExamples.title: World Economic Forum – First Mover Cities Cohort
illustrativeExamples.fullText: First Mover Cities is an emerging city cohort being developed within by the World Economic Forum, drawing on its First Movers Coalition, to explore approaches to intra-city aggregated purchasing power. It aims to bring together city governments, businesses across the supply and demand sides of the construction value chain, finance institutions and other partners to strengthen demand for low-carbon solutions. Initial work focuses on the built environment, with a particular focus on cement and concrete, using multistakeholder dialogues to exchange practical experience on green procurement approaches, governance, tender design and supplier engagement. These exchanges will also explore how cities can develop credible demand packages by coordinating public and private purchasing needs and commitments. Over time, this could inform approaches to intra-city aggregated purchasing and strengthen cities' ability to shape markets for low-carbon solutions. San Francisco, Boston, Oslo, Stockholm and Belém are the initial First Mover Cities, with ambitions to expand participation globally and potentially extend the approach to other urban value chains, such as mobility solutions.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: First Mover Cities shows how international public-private collaboration can help cities to explore intra-city aggregated purchasing power and strengthen their ability to shape markets for low-carbon solutions.

illustrativeExamples.title: World Bank – Global Platform for Sustainable Cities (GPSC)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Led by the World Bank and supported by the Global Environment Facility (GEF), GPSC provides knowledge exchange, capacity building, and practical tools to support integrated urban sustainability planning and investment. It supports the wider GEF Sustainable Cities Programme, which links a global knowledge platform with country-led, city-level projects financed through GEF resources and development-partner co-financing. This structure connects national and local urban priorities with international expertise, financing partners, and implementation support.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: GPSC shows how international partnerships can connect national and subnational governments with technical expertise, investment planning support, and development finance.

illustrativeExamples.title: UN-Habitat – RISE-UP
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Established by UN-Habitat, RISE-UP has worked with national and local governments through its global, regional, and country offices to connect urban resilience priorities with international financing partners. Through partnerships with the Adaptation Fund, Green Climate Fund, and bilateral agencies, including Sweden's Sida, RISE UP reports mobilizing over USD 150 million for urban climate resilience initiatives across nearly 30 countries. Although its flagship program concluded in 2025, the RISE UP portfolio continues supporting cities with financing readiness, institutional capacity, and implementation of resilience investments.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: Key takeaway: RISE-UP shows how international partnerships can connect national and local governments with climate finance and technical support for urban adaptation.

illustrativeExamples.title: AFD/IDFC – NDBs Urban Climate Action (NUCA)
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Developed by the International Development Finance Club (IDFC) Facility, with financial and technical support from the IKI International Climate Initiative and the Agence Française de Développement (AFD), the NUCA Programme (2024–2028) supports partnerships between development banks and cities across five countries. With a €20 million budget and 10 implementation partners, the programme aims to strengthen development banks' technical and institutional capacities, integrate climate considerations into urban financing frameworks, develop pipelines of bankable urban climate projects and mobilise investment for low-carbon, climate-resilient infrastructure. It also supports knowledge development and exchange among cities, development banks and other stakeholders, with a focus on more than 100 secondary cities.
illustrativeExamples.connectionLine: NUCA demonstrates how international partnerships can strengthen national and regional development banks' capacity to finance urban climate action and connect municipal investment needs with financing institutions.

howToUse.title: How to Use the Toolkit
howToUse.intro: The CHAMP Toolkit is designed primarily for national governments, working with cities and subnational authorities, Friends of CHAMP and development partners, to mobilize finance for implementation of urban and subnational climate action.

countryJourneys.tagline: Sweden: An Evolving Mission-Oriented Approach to Urban Climate Transition
countryJourneys.summary: Showcasing how Viable Cities, Climate City Contract 2030, the Coordination Function, and System Demonstrators form an interconnected multilevel delivery system spanning 48 municipalities and 6 national agencies.
countryJourneys.headerDescription: Sweden’s journey illustrates two central premises – 1) no actor can deliver the climate transition alone, and 2) finance becomes more effective when governance and implementation systems are in place to organize collective action.
countryJourneys.tabASubtitle: An Evolving Mission-Oriented Approach to Urban Climate Transition

contextSections.title: An Evolving, Iterative Multilevel Climate Action Model
paragraphs: Sweden's multilevel climate action model has evolved iteratively, as successive stages of climate action exposed new challenges and opportunities for financing, implementation, and coordination. This evolution has been shaped by strong municipal autonomy, a well-developed research and innovation system, established municipal financing capacity, and a governance culture that supports experimentation and learning across institutional boundaries.

contextSections.title: Municipalities as a "Gathering Force"
paragraphs: Sweden has 290 municipalities and 21 administrative regions, with municipalities enjoying substantial autonomy over local planning, public services and investment. Municipalities also own utilities and companies responsible for services such as district heating, water, waste management and housing, giving them an important role in local climate-related infrastructure investment. Yet many regulatory, financial and infrastructure conditions are determined nationally or at the European Union level, while businesses, utilities, property owners and citizens control important assets and decisions. A central premise of the Swedish approach is therefore that no single actor or level of government can deliver the transition alone. Municipalities can instead act as a “gathering force,” connecting their own mandates with actors whose decisions are also necessary for transition. This has encouraged a shift from traditional municipal governance toward more network-based, multilevel forms of governance and coordination.

contextSections.title: Viable Cities: A Country Platform Orchestrating the Swedish Ecosystem
paragraphs: Sweden's multilevel model developed through its mission-oriented innovation ecosystem. Viable Cities was established in 2017 and progressively brought municipalities, national agencies, research institutions, businesses, and civil society around the mission of climate-neutral cities by 2030. Rather than attempting national scale immediately, the program developed approaches with pioneer municipalities over time:

bulletPoints.text: 48 municipalities in 2024 (covering approximately half of Sweden's total population)

contextSections.title: Climate City Contracts: Integrating Climate Action into Coordination and Planning Process
paragraphs: As Viable Cities developed its mission of climate-neutral cities by 2030, it recognized the need for stronger political commitments and sustained cooperation between municipalities and national agencies. This led to the introduction of Climate City Contract 2030 (CCC) as an iterative governance process, alongside the development of Transition Arenas and, later, Samordningsfunktionen (the Coordination Function). Importantly, the emerging governance process was designed to interact with municipalities' ordinary planning, budgeting, and political cycles, and to be reviewed and renewed over time, rather than becoming a parallel climate-governance structure.

contextSections.title: System Demonstrators: Collaborative Implementation Environments
paragraphs: Sweden’s system demonstrator approach builds on earlier experience with innovation and pilots. It was progressively connected to the Climate City Contract process from 2021 and developed through staged funding calls from 2022. This experience also highlighted that technology alone was insufficient when policy, finance, business models and other conditions shaped implementation.

Viable Cities developed System Demonstrators to bring multiple actors and interventions together around bounded, real-world transition challenges and coordinated portfolios of action. Examples in Lund and Stockholm demonstrate this approach across areas including energy, mobility and transport. From 2021 onwards, System Demonstrators were progressively connected to the wider CCC process.

contextSections.title: Bridging the Financing Gap: Local Investment Structures & Viability Fund
paragraphs: As these governance and delivery approaches matured and accelerated action, new challenges emerged for matching finance with climate transition priorities. Urban transition portfolios can involve multiple owners, different risk and maturity profiles, and may require enabling interventions that are not themselves investable. These challenges prompted emerging work on Local Investment Structures to better connect local transition priorities with investment and finance.

This evolution reflects a second core principle emphasized by Viable Cities: finance follows governance. This does not mean that finance only enters after governance is complete. Rather, political direction, local ownership, coordination and portfolios create the conditions for financing needs to become clearer and for finance actors to engage. The financing challenge is therefore also a governance and implementation challenge: connecting actors, priorities, investment planning, finance, and procurement into a coherent system.

This thinking has also informed the emerging Viability Fund for Cities, reflecting Sweden's growing emphasis on connecting its established governance and implementation approaches with new financing and market-shaping arrangements.
Part B examines Sweden’s multilevel climate action model, including the mechanisms that emerged through this evolution and how they interact across the toolkit's five Actions.

countryJourneys.modelOverview:
Sweden's experience brings together mechanisms at different stages of maturity. Viable Cities, Climate City Contract 2030, the Coordination Function and System Demonstrators are established components, while Local Investment Structures, the Viability Fund for Cities and stronger aggregated-demand and financing interfaces are being developed. The diagram above illustrates how these arrangements connect within Sweden's multilevel climate action model.

Together, these mechanisms illustrate how the Toolkit's five reinforcing Actions contribute to CHAMP's three Implementation Roadmap pillars: strengthening multilevel climate governance (Pillar 1), catalyzing partnerships for local delivery (Pillar 2), and unlocking finance and investment at the subnational level (Pillar 3). In particular, Sweden demonstrates how country-level coordination and partnerships can connect local climate priorities with investment planning, financing and implementation, supported by continuous learning and institutional development.

actions.title: Action 1. Establish Multilevel Commitments and Platforms for Climate Investment
paragraphs: At the centre of Sweden's multilevel coordination model is the annual Climate City Contract 2030 (CCC) process, through which municipalities, national agencies and Viable Cities establish and renew complementary commitments. As part of this process, Transition Arenas mobilize local stakeholders, including businesses, academia and civil society, around shared priorities, while Joint Commitments enable groups of municipalities to collaborate on common governance and implementation challenges.

Viable Cities serves as Sweden's national coordination platform, connecting municipalities, six national agencies and wider transition actors. Its dedicated Coordination Function (discussed in Action 2) supports the CCC process and facilitates ongoing national–local collaboration. National agencies also use joint action planning to connect their commitments with national programmes, policy instruments and municipal implementation priorities.

Building on this experience, the emerging Viability Fund for Cities seeks to support urban climate transitions across countries by aligning implementation partners, facilitating financing partnerships and strengthening aggregated demand. Its architecture comprises three complementary segments:
actions.enabledSummary: What this has enabled: Sweden has established recurring mechanisms for shared commitments and national-local coordination, while developing new arrangements to connect these governance foundations with financing and market actors. The opportunity is to strengthen how these interconnected mechanisms translate local transition priorities into coordinated investment and implementation.

actions.title: Action 2. Strengthen Enabling Environments for Climate Investment
paragraphs: Sweden's Coordination Function (Samordningsfunktionen) plays an intermediary role in identifying institutional, governance and financing challenges affecting local climate action. Through analysis of municipal needs, dialogue and ongoing review, it identifies recurring challenges and areas where additional support or changes beyond the municipal level may be needed.

These insights can inform national agency discussions on how existing mandates, policy instruments and funding programmes could better support local implementation. This provides a channel for municipal experience to inform national-level coordination and identify opportunities to strengthen enabling conditions for climate investment. While Sweden’s Coordination Function does not integrate local priorities into NDCs or NAPs, such mechanisms could help countries bring subnational priorities into national climate planning and implementation, supporting the CHAMP Roadmap’s priorities under Pillars 1.2 and 2.1.
actions.enabledSummary: What this has enabled: Sweden has established an intermediary mechanism for bringing local implementation challenges into multilevel policy discussions. The opportunity is to use these insights to inform more targeted national support and improvements to the policy, institutional and financing conditions for local climate investment.

actions.title: Action 3. Plan and Prepare Climate Investments
paragraphs: Through the Climate City Contract (CCC) process, Swedish municipalities and their partners work to connect shared commitments with implementation portfolios, climate action plans and investment planning. The portfolio approach brings together interconnected interventions across infrastructure, policy, governance, procurement and capacity development. Climate investment planning helps to identify associated investment needs, indicative costs, financing sources and responsible actors.

Looking ahead, country-level coordination could connect locally owned investment portfolios with national climate finance strategies and investment plans (Roadmap 3.1). It could also connect these portfolios with coordinated project preparation support and finance partners (Roadmap 3.2), while investment decisions remain with the responsible owners and financiers.

Swedish municipalities participating in CCCs are working to integrate climate investment planning into ordinary planning and budgeting processes. Stockholm, for example, examines how existing municipal expenditure, procurement and investment decisions can contribute to climate objectives, alongside identifying additional climate-specific investments. However, the maturity of climate investment planning varies across participating municipalities, and extending its scope to encompass the wider public and private actors involved in urban transitions remains an area for further development.
actions.enabledSummary: What this has enabled: Sweden is progressively connecting climate commitments and implementation priorities with investment needs and municipal budgeting processes. The opportunity is to strengthen project preparation and coordination of investment portfolios across government levels, particularly for investments involving actors beyond municipal government.

actions.title: Action 4. Mobilize Finance and Shape Markets
paragraphs: Sweden is exploring Local Investment Structures to coordinate, prepare and finance investments within wider climate transition portfolios. The proposed model of these structures combines two complementary functions:

• Local Governance Function: Establishes the structure's mandate and accountability, coordinates participating investment owners, and agrees how responsibilities, costs, benefits, risks and investment decisions are shared.
• Local Investment Function: Prepares investment portfolios, structures financing and risks, and connects investments with suitable capital. Where appropriately mandated, it may also receive, manage and deploy capital, including managing repayments and reinvestment.

These structures require clear arrangements for ownership, investment decision-making, capital management and connections to national and international finance. Their functions can be delivered through different institutional arrangements, including municipal balance sheets, public banks, funds or dedicated investment vehicles, depending on local mandates and legal conditions.

EnergyNet is an open-protocol approach to local energy systems, allowing different providers to develop compatible solutions and services using a shared Energy Protocol. Its first application in Brunnshög was developed through CoAction Lund, involving municipal property owners and ViaEuropa as an early technology developer. EnergyNet is being explored as a use case for Local Investment Structures to coordinate investment preparation and financing across multiple owners, including agreements on responsibilities and the sharing of costs, benefits and risks. The proposed co-financing arrangements remain under development.

Alongside financing, Sweden is developing approaches to intra-city aggregated purchasing and market shaping, where cities convene public and private buyers around shared climate outcomes while each participating buyer retains its own budget and purchasing decisions. By coordinating purchasing requirements, anticipated volumes and timelines, cities can create credible demand signals that encourage suppliers to invest in low-carbon solutions, helping mobilize additional investment for climate action. Sweden, through Viable Cities, supports the World Economic Forum’s development of the First Mover Cities cohort, with Stockholm participating as one of the cities. The cohort initially focuses on coordinating demand for low-carbon cement and concrete.
actions.enabledSummary: What this is enabling: Sweden is strengthening the foundations for connecting local climate investments with suitable financing and coordinated market demand. The opportunity is to further develop these emerging arrangements to mobilize capital, support implementation and create stronger markets for climate solutions.

actions.title: Action 5. Learn, Strengthen Capacities and Scale Implementation
paragraphs: System Demonstrators generate practical learning about the governance arrangements, institutional capabilities and partnerships needed to implement and scale systemic urban transitions. Experiences from Lund and Stockholm can inform subsequent interventions and help other municipalities adapt effective approaches to their own contexts.

Learning is also embedded in the annual Climate City Contract (CCC) renewal process, through which municipalities and national agencies review commitments, progress and implementation experience to inform subsequent cycles. While this is not a formal national reporting mechanism, similar approaches could inform voluntary country-led reviews of multilevel climate action, as envisaged under the CHAMP Implementation Roadmap (1.3).

Sweden is also working to extend this learning internationally through collaborations aimed at developing shared principles and methodologies for System Demonstrator programs (see Further Resources). These efforts seek to connect cities, funders and implementation partners around common approaches to programme design, experimentation and evaluation, while enabling lessons to be adapted across different institutional and country contexts.
actions.enabledSummary: What this has enabled: Sweden has established practical environments for collaborative experimentation and learning, generating insights that can inform wider implementation. The opportunity is to translate this experience into stronger institutional capacities, sustained funding and approaches that can be replicated and adapted across cities and countries.

contextSections.title: Decentralized Urban Responsibilities and Federal Investments
paragraphs: Brazil's multilevel climate investment system builds on its longstanding federal structure. The 1988 [Constitution](https://www.stf.jus.br/arquivo/cms/legislacaoConstituicao/anexo/brazil_federal_constitution.pdf) established municipalities as autonomous federative entities alongside the federal government and states, assigning them substantial responsibilities for urban planning, infrastructure and public services. However, municipal fiscal capacities remain highly uneven; larger municipalities have [stronger own-source revenues and borrowing capacities](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-41283-7_5), while smaller municipalities often depend more heavily on intergovernmental transfers and face greater technical and financial constraints.

Brazil has established federal institutions and programmes to support urban infrastructure investment. The Ministry of Cities was established in 2003, while the [Growth Acceleration Programme (PAC)](https://www.gov.br/empresas-e-negocios/pt-br/invest-export-brasil/investir/encontre-oportunidades-de-investimentos/pac), launched in 2007, strengthened [federal support for state and municipal investments](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2007/lei/l11578.htm). Additionally, established public financial institutions, including [BNDES](https://economia.lse.ac.uk/articles/10.31389/eco.519) and [CAIXA](https://www.caixa.gov.br/poder-publico/modernizacao-gestao/pro-cidades/Paginas/default.aspx), also play an important role in Brazil's urban investment architecture.

contextSections.title: Developing Climate Policy and Subnational Leadership
paragraphs: Alongside this urban investment architecture, Brazil progressively developed national climate policy and dedicated financing mechanisms. The [National Policy on Climate Change](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2007-2010/2009/lei/l12187.htm), established a framework for mitigation and adaptation, while the creation of the [National Climate Fund](https://www.gov.br/mma/pt-br/composicao/secex/dfre/fundo-nacional-sobre-mudanca-do-clima) (Fundo Clima), both adopted in 2009, introduced a dedicated source of climate financing. Brazil's first National Adaptation Plan followed in 2016.

States and municipalities also exercised climate leadership. For example, the city and state of São Paulo adopted [climate legislation](https://legislacao.prefeitura.sp.gov.br/lei-14933-de-05-de-junho-de-2009/consolidado) in 2009, while cities including [Recife, Belo Horizonte and Curitiba](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009249676.004) developed their own climate policies and coordination mechanisms. These developments reflected the scope for subnational climate action within Brazil's federal system.

contextSections.title: Renewing Multilevel Coordination and Formalizing Climate Federalism
paragraphs: Brazil's renewed climate agenda in 2023, with the creation of [interministerial coordination](https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2023-2026/2023/decreto/D11550.htm) bodies for climate action and [multilevel governance coordination](https://www2.camara.leg.br/legin/fed/decret/2024/decreto-12040-5-junho-2024-795719-publicacaooriginal-171971-pe.html) mechanisms, placed greater emphasis on coordinating climate action across government levels. The Ministry of Cities was re-established, alongside the relaunch of the Growth Acceleration Programme as [Novo PAC](https://www.gov.br/cidades/pt-br/acesso-a-informacao/acoes-e-programas/pac).

A significant milestone followed in July 2024, when federal, state and municipal governments adopted the [Commitment to Climate Federalism](https://ses.sp.bvs.br/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/U_RS-PR-CF-3_030724.pdf) through the Federation Council, building on Brazil's endorsement of CHAMP. [Plano Clima 2024–2035](https://www.gov.br/mma/pt-br/composicao/smc/plano-clima-1), formally launched in 2026, further developed Brazil's national framework for mitigation and adaptation. It includes Cities Sector Plans for mitigation and adaptation, linking national climate priorities with urban planning, sustainable mobility and resilient infrastructure.
